POLICY CONTEXT / CANADA

On October 23, 2026, the Trump administration announced an expansion of its additional 50% Section 338 tariff on covered Canadian-origin goods, adding the five medical technology and related categories shown here, effective October 30, 2026. Together, these categories accounted for US$1.024 billion in U.S. imports from Canada in 2025.

This additional tariff is Canada-specific. It does not impose the same duty on goods originating in the other countries shown in the charts. Those goods may face separate tariffs. The announcement covers a broader list of products; these five categories are this dashboard’s selected focus.

The 2025 value is a historical trade baseline, not tariff revenue or a measurement of imports that paid the duty. The displayed January–September 2026 data predate this expansion. Product coverage and exceptions follow the official tariff provisions.

October 23 proclamation ↗Official product annexes and effective date ↗

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR CONSUMERS

Medical products covered by the tariff.

Many of these products are bought by laboratories, hospitals and training centres rather than directly by shoppers. They help professionals run tests, check results, perform surgery and practise essential skills.

Putting the trade value in perspective

The five categories accounted for US$1.024 billion in U.S. imports from Canada in 2025. Converted to Canadian dollars, that gross trade value was equivalent to approximately 0.044% of Canada’s 2025 nominal GDP. This comparison describes the scale of the trade; it does not measure GDP lost, tariff payments or the economic cost of the tariff.

Calculation and sources

US$1.024222992 billion × C$1.3978 per US$1 = approximately C$1.431659 billion. Dividing by C$3,245.257 billion in nominal GDP and multiplying by 100 gives 0.044115%, rounded to 0.044%.

The numerator is the full 2025 customs value of these categories, before determining exemptions or duty paid on individual shipments. Exchange rate: Bank of Canada, 2025 annual average. GDP: IMF nominal GDP series distributed through FRED, 2025 observation of C$3,245,257 million. GDP observations may be revised.

REFERENCE MATERIALS / SHIPPING

Some laboratory supplies need special handling

The National Research Council says some reference materials require dry ice during transport, adding a C$75 charge per order, not per product. This is an NRC shipping charge, separate from customs tariffs.

NRC’s ANGII-1 is a certified reference material of angiotensin II. Its listing illustrates a laboratory reference product; it does not establish that this particular item needs dry ice or that it appears in the trade records. See the NRC catalog and shipping note.

What this means for consumers

Why supply chains matter

A medical product can depend on materials, components and expertise from several countries. The OECD finds that international sourcing has helped make medical products more affordable and given buyers more sourcing options. Disruptions can still travel through those connections.

How a tariff can reach consumers

An additional import duty can raise the cost of bringing a covered product into the United States. Depending on how suppliers and buyers respond, that cost could affect purchasing budgets or prices further along the supply chain. A 50% import duty does not automatically mean a 50% increase in a patient’s bill.

What the country shares tell you

The charts show where U.S. imports come from. A larger country share means more import value comes from that source. It does not tell us whether another supplier can make an equivalent product, how quickly buyers could switch, or whether a shortage will occur.

Supply-chain background: OECD (2024), Securing Medical Supply Chains in a Post-Pandemic World. This report provides general context; it does not evaluate this tariff’s effects. The dashboard’s data do not establish changes in patient prices, waiting times or availability.

04 / SOURCES & METHODS

Transparent by design.

This is a reproducible snapshot of USITC DataWeb, compiled from official U.S. Census Bureau merchandise trade statistics. It does not refresh automatically.

Open USITC DataWeb ↗Original Excel export ↓Structured data (JSON) ↓
What is included?

Imports for consumption; customs value in actual U.S. dollars; HTS8; all countries, programs, provision codes and districts. Countries and commodities are reported separately. Annual 2025 and January–September 2025/2026 are available. The source’s incomplete annual 2026 column is excluded.

How are the measures calculated?

Country share = country import value ÷ all-country import value within the same HTS code and period. CR3 = the sum of the three largest shares. Country HHI = sum of squared percentage shares across all countries. Ranks include positive-value countries only. Year-over-year changes compare January–September in both years.

What can’t these figures tell us?

Country HHI is not firm HHI. Countries may contain related manufacturers, and goods within a code may not be substitutes. Imports exclude domestic production, so shares are not shares of U.S. consumption. These trade data do not identify affected companies, establish duty paid on individual shipments, or attribute trade changes to tariffs. The policy summary links to the separate legal sources for tariff coverage. HTS 90230000 and 90273080 include nonmedical uses. Nominal import values combine price, volume and product-mix changes.

Where do the category examples come from?

Examples explain typical uses and do not identify the products or brands in the trade data. Classification depends on the particular item. References: WCO diagnostic test classifications; CBP reagent example; NRC reference materials; CBP electrosurgical guidance; CBP demonstration models; and USITC tariff definitions.

Canadian medical-device market context

The International Trade Administration describes Canada as the world’s eighth-largest medical-device market, estimated at US$9.8 billion in 2024, and reports a projected compound annual growth rate of 5.5%. These figures describe the broader Canadian market, while this dashboard focuses on five selected U.S. import categories.

Source: International Trade Administration, Canada — Medical Devices. The growth rate is a forecast, not an observed result.

How can I reproduce the results?

Download the original workbook above, or query DataWeb with the displayed five HTS8 codes, imports for consumption, customs value, all countries separately, and annual plus year-to-date reporting. The CSV contains the complete extracted country observations. All chart and table statistics are calculated from those observations.
